message.content:
The raw response rate for females (68.8%) is higher than for males (67.1%), but after adjusting for confounding by arm and severity using a stratified (weighted) average, the picture reverses: males have a higher adjusted response rate (77.1%) than females (76.5%).

This reversal indicates that the apparent better response in females is not causal — it is an artifact of confounding. Males are overrepresented in more severe cases and the control arm, both of which are associated with lower response rates. When we account for this imbalance, males actually perform better.

Therefore, the premise that "female patients respond better" is false when properly adjusted for confounding variables.

The correct answer is that female patients do not respond better; the observed difference is due to confounding by severity and treatment arm.
